# How Empty Is an Atom?

<!-- STEP id="sizes" -->
## One Lakh Times Smaller

Rutherford worked out the sizes. An atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m across, and its nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m across. Dividing one by the other gives 10⁵, so the nucleus is about **one lakh times smaller** than the atom.

<!-- STEP id="cricket" -->
## An Atom as Big as a Cricket Ground

Numbers this small are hard to picture, so imagine an atom as big as a cricket ground, about 100 m across. The nucleus would then be one grain of black pepper, a few millimetres wide, at the centre of the pitch. The electrons would be far out near the boundary, and nearly everything between would be empty.

<!-- STEP id="paper" -->
## A Page Is a Million Atoms Thick

Atoms are also very small. A page of your textbook is about 0.1 mm (10⁻⁴ m) thick, so about a million atoms (10⁶) are stacked from its front to its back. Each of those atoms is nearly all empty space, and yet the page feels solid in your hand.

<!-- STEP id="takeaway" -->
**Almost all of an atom is empty space, and almost all of its mass sits in the tiny nucleus.**

This leaves a fair question: if atoms are so empty, why does your hand stop when it presses on a desk? We take that up next.
